content: # Unescape or HTML Decode: When Twig Protects You Too Much It happens frequently in full-stack development, particularly when integrating legacy backends with modern templating engines. You are rendering data from a PHP controller that has already prepared clean strings for the browser. However, upon switching to Twig, those same values suddenly appear double-encoded: `<a href='...` instead of the expected ``. This occurs because Twig treats all output by default as untrusted data. When you use the standard `{{ item.Link }}` syntax, Twig automatically applies HTML escaping to prevent Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. It converts characters like `<`, `>`, and `'` into their HTML entity equivalents. If your backend logic assumes Twig will render raw HTML, this automatic protection breaks the layout and renders tags as plain text. The solution depends entirely on the trustworthiness of your data source. You cannot simply apply a blanket "unescape" strategy without understanding the security implications. ### The Security Trade-off: `raw` vs. `escape` If you confirm that the data in `item.Link` is safeâmeaning it originated from a trusted database column that never accepts user input directly, or has been sanitized on the server side before reaching Twigâyou can bypass the automatic escaping filter. In Twig 1.12.2 and later versions, you must explicitly tell the template engine to treat the variable as trusted HTML. You do this by appending the `|raw` filter: ```twig {{ item.Link | raw }} ``` This instruction tells Twig: "Do not convert `<` or `>` into `<` and `>`; print them exactly as they are." This restores the intended HTML structure without requiring any changes to your PHP backend. ### When You Need `escape_html` Explicitly The inverse scenario is equally common but often misunderstood.
